problem: The text says the gain falls at 20 dB per decade 'above the corner f = 1/(2πR₁C)'. For an ideal integrator the magnitude falls at 20 dB per decade at every frequency; the corner is only the point where the gain passes through 1 (0 dB). As written, a student may think the gain is flat below the corner, which is true of the practical circuit in Section 2, not the ideal one.
fix: Write: 'The gain magnitude is 1/(ωR₁C) and falls at 20 dB per decade at all frequencies; it equals 1 (0 dB) at f = 1/(2πR₁C), the corner frequency.'

problem: 'A sine input gives a cosine output, shifted by 90°' drops the minus sign from vout = −RC dvin/dt. The true output for vin = V sin(ωt) is −RCω cos(ωt), an inverted cosine, i.e. the output lags the input by 90°. A student reading only this sentence will sketch a plain +cosine.
fix: Write: 'For vin = V sin(ωt), vout = −RCω cos(ωt): the output is a cosine of amplitude RCω, inverted, so it lags the input by 90°.'

problem: The sample points for both series are spaced 1250 Hz apart on a linear grid, so the first plotted point is at about 1.25 kHz. On a 1 Hz to 100 kHz log axis the integrator line and the differentiator line are drawn only in the right-hand part of the plot; the whole 1 Hz to 1.25 kHz region has no curve, so the figure does not show the low-frequency behaviour it describes.
fix: Sample the frequencies on a logarithmic grid, for example 20 points per decade from 1 Hz to 100 kHz, so both lines are drawn across the full axis (clipping only where the gain goes outside the −60 dB to +60 dB window).
